items.title: Perception of English /iː/–/ɪ/ by Japanese Listeners under Silent-Centre and Devoiced Vowel Conditions
items.abstract: This study examined Japanese listeners' perception of the English /iː/-/ɪ/ contrast under 'silent-centre' and devoiced vowel conditions, extending previous 'silent-centre' research by incorporating vowel devoicing and aspiration. The results show that L2 vowel perception is strongly shaped by L1 Japanese phonological knowledge, particularly duration-based effects and clipping-induced effects linked to gemination. Contrary to prediction, stimuli with high-frequency components of the devoiced vowel and the presence of aspiration did not improve identification accuracy. Instead, Japanese listeners with lower English proficiency appeared not to exploit spectral information associated with devoicing or aspiration, which is consistent with earlier findings.

items.title: Applying the Simplified Vocal Profile Analysis to Swiss German Dialects
items.authors: Alessia Wüst(University of Berne); Adrian Leemann(University of Berne)
items.abstract: This work presents the first perceptual investigation of vocal profiles in Swiss German, utilizing data from 127 speakers (aged 18-40) from the Swiss Dialäktatlas. Using Simplified Vocal Profile Analysis, four coders assessed vocal profiles to map geographic and social trends. While inter-rater reliability proved challenging (κ=0.09-0.39), consensus coding revealed clear stratification. Regarding gender, men typically exhibited a relaxed vocal tract ('hypoarticulation'), whereas women showed a tendency toward pharyngeal expansion ('hyperarticulation'). Geographically, Northeast Switzerland is characterized by nasality, while Central Switzerland is marked by pharyngeal expansion - a finding likely confounded by the gender distribution in the sample. Notably, creaky voice remains rare in Swiss German. These results suggest that while vocal profiles function as salient markers of regional and social identity, methodological complexities call for refined protocols in future research.

items.title: The Role of Context and Prosody in the Understanding of English Irony by Chinese L2 Learners
items.authors: Yinan Lin(Nanjing University of Science and Technology); Shanpeng Li(Nanjing University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Irony conveys a meaning opposite to its literal expression and is frequently used for humorous, critical, or satirical purposes. Because of its ambiguity, ironic interpretation relies heavily on contextual cues and prosodic features. However, the interplay between context and prosody in second language (L2) irony comprehension remains unclear. This study investigates their relative contributions and examines whether language proficiency affects Chinese English learners’ ability to interpret irony. A perception experiment was conducted using English materials with three contextual and three prosodic conditions. Results showed that context played a dominant role in irony comprehension, while prosody contributed independently when contextual information was limited. Language proficiency had only a minor effect. The findings support the Parallel Constraint Satisfaction Model and offer implications for irony research and English language teaching.

items.title: Cross-linguistic word-medial stop lenition: A Functional PCA approach
items.authors: Seung Suk Lee(McGill University); Morgan Sonderegger(McGill University); Meghan Clayards(McGill University)
items.abstract: Stop lenition between vowels is pervasive, yet fundamental questions remain: to what extent is lenition the same phenomenon across languages, and does it serve a common function? The continuity lenition hypothesis proposes one: weakened stops signal prosodic continuation and aid word segmentation. Previous work supports this idea but has examined few languages with differing methods, limiting cross-linguistic generalizability. We investigate word-medial continuity lenition in large speech corpora across nine languages, using Functional PCA of intensity contours to quantify the degree of lenition. We find a near-universal tendency for word-medial stops to be weaker, with voiced stops most consistent across languages. Exceptions reflect language-specific phonology or corpus artifacts, supporting continuity lenition as a cross-linguistic segmentation cue. Languages vary in whether weakening affects duration and/or intensity, suggesting listeners must learn cue patterns in their language.

items.title: Beyond Speaker Independence: Evaluating Cross-Lingual Acoustic-to-Articulatory Inversion Across Finnish and Russian
items.authors: Ruchi Pandey(University of Eastern Finland); Tomi H. Kinnunen(University of Eastern Finland)
items.abstract: Acoustic-to-articulatory inversion (AAI) remains challenging under domain shifts where changes in speaker attributes and cross-language conditions often degrade performance. We conduct a systematic evaluation under such shifts and establish baseline benchmarks on FROST-EMA, a Finnish-Russian bilingual EMA corpus. FROST-EMA addresses the English bias and limited speaker diversity of existing resources. We benchmark (i) articulatory targets (raw EMA coordinates vs tract variables), (ii) acoustic front-ends (MFCC vs SSL features), and (iii) inversion back-ends (BiLSTM vs a lightweight attention-based sequence model). We further define evaluation protocols for cross-gender transfer (within language) and cross-language transfer (within gender). The results indicate that cross-gender mismatch introduces moderate Pearson correlation declines (approx. 0.05--0.10) relative to the in-domain baseline, whereas cross-language mismatch causes larger drops (approx 0.10- 0.20).

items.title: L2 Speakers Accommodate Differently to AI and Human Voices Across Phonetic Features
items.authors: Nan Gan(University of Zurich); Elisa Pellegrino(University of Zurich)
items.abstract: Phonetic accommodation refers to speakers' adjustment of acoustic-phonetic patterns toward a speech model. Prior work comparing accommodation to human and AI voices has rarely included L2 populations and typically examined a narrow set of phonetic features. This study investigated the accommodation of 28 L1 Mandarin learners of L2 English to a Microsoft Azure TTS-generated voice and a native human voice in a sentence-shadowing task. Acoustic analyses targeted stop-consonant voice onset time (VOT), the tense-lax contrast /i/-/I/ in duration and spectral distance, and speech rhythm. Results showed stronger VOT convergence toward the human voice, but greater adjustment in vowel duration contrast and rhythm toward the AI voice, with no difference in vowel spectral contrast. These findings suggest that model-type effects on L2 phonetic accommodation are feature-dependent and AI and human voices may play complementary roles in supporting L2 phonetic acquisition.

items.title: Disentangling sociophonetic and physiological variation in /s/ acoustics across 12 languages
items.authors: Massimo Lipari(McGill University); Morgan Sonderegger(McGill University); Meghan Clayards(McGill University)
items.abstract: Sibilants, especially /s/, display gendered variation across languages. From acoustic data alone, it can be hard to determine whether this variation is due to performance of social identity or to physiology, e.g. vocal tract length (VTL) variation. In causal terms, there is a direct effect of gender on sibilant acoustics and an indirect effect mediated by VTL, which must be teased apart. To this end, a speaker's VTL can be estimated from their vowel formants, though the consistency of this measure's relationship to sibilant acoustics is largely untested. Using a new multilingual phonetic database of 12 languages (>1,300 speakers) and the tools of causal mediation analysis, we investigate the relationship between VTL and /s/ peak frequency and its causal role in gender effects. We find that estimated VTL predicts peak well across languages. While there are gender differences in peak across nearly all languages, the relative contributions of physiology and performance vary considerably.

items.title: From Rhythm Metrics to Latent Embeddings: Categorising English and Hindi Varieties in Northeast India
items.authors: John Aheibam(Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati); Joyshree Chakraborty(Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati); Priyankoo Sarmah(Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati); Rohit Sinha(Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati)
items.abstract: This study examines speech rhythm across English varieties spoken in Northeast (NE) India using traditional rhythm metrics and computational speech approaches. The dataset includes five NE Indian English varieties from different L1 backgrounds, viz. Angami, Assamese, Khasi, Meiteilon, and Mizo, together with two Hindi varieties spoken by native Hindi speakers and Assamese speakers. Durational rhythm measures were used to investigate language grouping patterns and served as features for the linear mixed-effects models, Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering, and Support Vector Machine analyses. The results revealed considerable overlap among the NE Indian English varieties, whereas the Hindi varieties were more clearly separated. Latent embedding vectors also showed a clear separation between Hindi and English varieties, while the NE Indian Englishes overlapped. A strong correlation between %V and PC1 suggests that temporal rhythmic patterns are partially captured in the embeddings.
